title: The Smiley, Stubborn Llama
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (with Ben sitting in for Jerry) discuss llamas: their origins in North America and relation to camels, domestication from guanacos in the Andes, physical traits and speed, pack-animal capacity (including Inca silver mining at Potosi), herd social structure, behavior and vocalizations, fleece and the lost Kashmir-quality fiber, Andean ritual and cultural significance, and llama antibodies (nanobodies) used in HIV, COVID-19 and biosensor research. The episode closes with tour dates announcement and contact information.

segments.title: Opening banter: Ben, Rim tribute show, and llama farm
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck, with Ben sitting in for Jerry, chat about a Athens, Georgia Replacements-style tribute show (Rim tribute show) Josh attended and a past llama farm connection, leading into the llama topic.

segments.title: Llama origins and domestication
segments.summary: Chuck explains that llamas were introduced to the US attempt in 1914 (a diseased llama meant for William Jennings Bryan was refused entry). Josh notes llama-like camelids originated in North America about 40 million years ago and dispersed to South America; they died out in North America at the end of the last Ice Age. Lamas are camelids related to camels, which also originated in North America. Llamas were domesticated in the Andes of Peru 4,000 to 5,000 years ago and were bred from guanacos, never existing in the wild.

segments.title: Llama family and relatives
segments.summary: The hosts describe the llama-family animals: guanacos, vicunas, alpacas and llamas, all camelids. They discuss uses for meat, tallow, hides, and dung for fuel, and note llamas were the only large domesticated animal in the ancient Americas.

segments.title: Llama physical traits and speed
segments.summary: Llamas are about four feet at the shoulder, males weigh 300 to 400 pounds, females 230 to 350 pounds. They have split upper lips, big ears, panoramic vision, and are aggressive toward predators. They can reach about 40 miles per hour.

segments.title: Llama feet and surefootedness
segments.summary: Llamas have soft padded, split toe feet rather than hooves, which lets them grip rocks and stay surefooted on mountains without tearing up slopes.

segments.title: Llamas as pack animals and Inca silver mining
segments.summary: Llamas carry about 100 to 135 pounds for 15 to 20 miles a day. They could not pull machines or carts, even with a wheel. A Spanish observer estimated the Inca used about 300,000 llamas to transport silver ore from Potosi mine in present-day Bolivia.

segments.title: Llama thirst tolerance, diet, and herd structure
segments.summary: Llamas tolerate thirst, eat varied shrubs, and have high-hemoglobin blood suited to high dry elevations. They are gregarious and live in family groups of one male, several females, and their offspring. The dominant male is territorial and drives off rival bachelor males.

segments.title: Llama communication, protective behavior, and stubbornness
segments.summary: Llamas adopt and protect other species such as sheep from predators. They communicate through body language and ear position, are quiet, hum to babies, and vocalize alarm that sounds like a scraped fork. They can be stubborn, spitting, hissing or kicking when overloaded or mistreated.

segments.title: Weaning, mating, and birth
segments.summary: The dominant male chases off young after about one year, to avoid competition and inbreeding. Llamas have an induced ovulation and gestation of about 11 months, one baby at a time, weighing 18 to 20 pounds. Crias can stand within the first hour and live around 15 years on average.

segments.title: Film recommendation: LAMB
segments.summary: Chuck recommends the A24 film LAMB, which he watched mostly in Icelandic with no subtitles. Josh says he plans to watch it.

segments.title: Lama children's book
segments.summary: Josh mentions a kids' book series called Llama Llama, and the hosts joke about the books' content.

segments.title: Llama fleece and lost Andean fiber
segments.summary: Llamas are shorn about every two years, yielding six and a half to seven and a half pounds of fiber, coarser than alpaca. Chuck cites a historian's work on mummified llamas found in Inca burial sites, which had fleece on par with Kashmir; the fleece was lost as the Spanish bred llamas for meat.

segments.title: Inca and Andean ritual and llama culture
segments.summary: Inca buried and sacrificed llamas on claimed land and ate them at community celebrations to honor gods. Andean herders still revere llamas, dress them up in parades in Bolivia, and some hold ceremonial llama marriages, which select for docile animals.

segments.title: Kashmir goat and Black Philip tangent
segments.summary: The hosts ask what Kashmir is and Chuck says it is from a Kashmir goat. They joke about the goat Black Philip from The Witch, with Chuck's claim that Black Philip was a Kashmir goat being a false claim he admits was a lie.

segments.title: Llama antibodies: HIV, COVID-19, and biosensors
segments.summary: Llama antibodies have only two heavy chains rather than four, making them smaller, sturdier and able to reach tiny viral receptor sites. They neutralize all sixty HIV strains tested and may bind SARS-CoV-2. Llama-derived nanobodies are used in biosensors to detect biological warfare agents, since human antibodies are fragile and expensive. Hosts note ethical concerns about animal research but say the llamas are treated well.

segments.title: Llama body language and personal party anecdotes
segments.summary: Chuck explains that forward-leaning ears signal curiosity. Josh and Chuck recall llamas at kids' birthday parties, including Chuck's thirty-fifth birthday petting zoo with McDonald's and Taco Bell.

segments.title: Tour dates and sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts announce 2024 tour dates including Medford MA, Washington DC, New York City Town Hall, Chicago, Minneapolis, Indianapolis, Durham NC and Atlanta, advise buying tickets only from official venue sites, and give the contact email and iHeartRadio credit.
